title: Blessed is the one who spoke
hookLine: the opening blessing praises the one who spoke and the world came to be

cards: Words make things happen. A judge says guilty, and a life changes. Two people say I do, and they're married.
A friend says I'm sorry, and something heals. Most of the time, though, our words are cheap. We say we'll call and don't.
We say five minutes and mean twenty. Now imagine a speaker whose every word becomes real, at once, with no gap. In many synagogues the room stands up for the blessing that praises exactly that.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO SPOKE, AND THE WORLD WAS.
teach.b: It begins: baruch she'amar v'hayah ha'olam, blessed is the one who spoke, and the world came to be. It points back to the Torah's first page.
In the old Jewish translation: "And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light." No tools, no raw materials in the story. Just speech, and then the world.
Then the blessing builds, line after line, each starting with baruch, blessed. Blessed is the one who makes creation. Who says and does.
Who decrees and fulfills. Who has mercy on the earth. Who has mercy on the creatures.
Who rewards those who revere him. Who lives forever. Who redeems and rescues.

teach.h: MERCY ON THE EARTH AND CREATURES.
teach.b: Notice two lines in the middle: mercy on the earth, and mercy on the creatures. The world isn't spoken into being and left; the same voice keeps caring for it. Customs gather around this blessing.

Many who wear a prayer shawl hold its two front fringes during the blessing and kiss them at the end. A late tradition says the text came down from heaven on a written note, and that its words number eighty-seven.
Whatever its history, it opens the songs with the most basic praise there is: the world exists because someone spoke, and kept their word.

how: Baruch She'amar opens the verses of song in the morning service; in many communities people stand for it, and those wearing a tallit hold the two front fringes and kiss them at the closing blessing.

games.q: you're opening a long stretch of praise. what's the first thing you praise God for?
o: for speaking, and the world coming to be.
games.why: blessed is the one who spoke, and the world came to be. the songs open at the very beginning: creation by speech.

practice: Think of one thing you're about to start, a project, a meal, a conversation, a week, and put a pause before its first moment.
If you pray, say baruch she'amar v'hayah ha'olam, blessed is the one who spoke and the world came to be; if not, notice that this new thing also begins with words.
Then bring to mind one promise you've made lately, and decide to keep it.
